name: Deep Half Guard
description: Master Deep Half Guard in BJJ. Advanced leverage-based guard with powerful sweeps, back takes, and submission options. Covers bottom and top perspectives with decision trees and success rates.
variant_uniqueness: Inverted leverage trades exposure for sweeps
overview:
Deep Half Guard is an advanced guard position where the bottom player positions themselves underneath one of the opponent's legs, creating a powerful leverage point for sweeps and back takes. Unlike traditional half guard where the opponent's leg is trapped between the bottom player's legs, deep half involves the bottom player getting their entire upper body underneath the opponent's center of gravity, often with the shoulder positioned at the opponent's far hip. This position offers exceptional sweeping leverage and is particularly effective for smaller practitioners against larger opponents.

The deep half guard represents a fundamental shift in guard philosophy, moving from traditional frames and distance management to an inverted leverage-based approach. By positioning underneath the opponent's center of gravity, the bottom player gains mechanical advantage that transcends size and strength differences. The position is characterized by extreme proximity and connection, with the bottom player using their entire body as a lever to disrupt the opponent's base. This creates opportunities for powerful sweeps that can lead directly to dominant positions or back control.

From the top perspective, deep half guard presents a deceptive challenge - while you appear to be winning because you're on top, the bottom player has created a sophisticated lever system using your body weight against you. Understanding the sweep mechanics from both perspectives is essential for modern BJJ practitioners, as this position has become a cornerstone of competitive grappling at all levels.
key_principles: Deep underhook control is the primary mechanism for sweeps and back takes
Bottom player creates fulcrum with shoulder and head against opponent's hip
Top player must manage weight distribution to prevent both waiter and Homer Simpson sweeps
Inverted positioning underneath center of gravity generates powerful leverage
Patient methodical movement trumps explosive attempts from both perspectives
Crossface control is critical defensive tool for top player
Position favors offense for bottom player despite appearing defensive

faq.question: What is Deep Half Guard in BJJ?
faq.answer: Deep Half Guard is an advanced BJJ guard position where the bottom player slides their entire upper body underneath the opponent's hips, controlling the opponent's far leg with a deep underhook. The bottom player's head and shoulder create a wedge against the opponent's inner thigh, generating powerful mechanical leverage for sweeps directly to Mount or Back Control. Despite appearing defensive, it is highly offensive.

faq.question: Is Deep Half Guard effective in competition?
faq.answer: Deep Half Guard is highly effective at all competition levels, especially in no-gi where grip restrictions make it harder to defend. Bernardo Faria won multiple IBJJF World Championships using Deep Half as his primary guard system. Success rates range from beginner 30% to advanced 65% for sweeps. The position becomes more effective as practitioners develop precise entry timing and sweep chain fluency.

faq.question: What are the main sweeps from Deep Half Guard?
faq.answer: The four primary sweeps are: (1) Waiter Sweep to Mount — drive forward pressure; (2) Old School Sweep to Side Control — classic hip-lift; (3) Rolling Back Take to Back Control — when opponent steps over; (4) X-Guard Sweep to standing — when opponent retreats their far leg. Each targets a different defensive reaction, creating a complete dilemma system.

faq.question: How does Deep Half Guard compare to regular Half Guard?
faq.answer: Regular Half Guard uses side-facing control from a more upright position. Deep Half Guard requires full inversion underneath the opponent's hips with a far-leg underhook. Deep Half creates superior sweeping leverage at the cost of greater positional exposure during entry. It is more specialized and offensive but has a steeper learning curve, typically suited to blue belt and above.

bottom.name: Deep Half Guard Bottom
bottom.description: Master Deep Half Guard Bottom with powerful sweeps, back takes, and leverage-based attacks. Success rates: Beginner 30%, Intermediate 50%, Advanced 65%.
bottom.overview:
Deep Half Guard Bottom is an advanced guard position where the bottom player wedges underneath the opponent's hips with deep underhook control of the far leg. This position creates powerful leverage for sweeps and back takes by controlling the opponent's base from below. The bottom player's head is positioned near the opponent's far hip, with their body inverted underneath, creating a stable platform for offensive attacks.

This position is particularly effective against pressure passers who commit their weight forward, as it uses their momentum against them. The deep underhook of the far leg combined with the wedge created by the bottom player's shoulder and head disrupts the top player's base completely. From here, the bottom player can execute powerful hip-lift sweeps, waiter sweeps, and transitions to the back.

Deep Half Guard Bottom requires excellent hip mobility, core strength, and timing to enter and maintain. While it appears defensive, it is actually a highly offensive position with multiple pathways to dominant positions. The position is a cornerstone of modern no-gi grappling and has been refined by practitioners like Jeff Glover, Lucas Leite, and Bernardo Faria into a comprehensive attacking system.

Deep underhook of opponent's far leg with bottom player's arm wrapped around the thigh, controlling the leg close to the body

Opponent's near leg typically controlled or monitored by bottom player's free hand or legs to prevent step-over passes
Bottom player's hips mobile and ready to elevate, creating constant pressure on opponent's base and balance

Deep underhook established on opponent's far leg before fully committing to position

Keep head and shoulder wedged against opponent's inner thigh to disrupt their base
Stay inverted underneath opponent's hips to maximize leverage for sweeps
Control or monitor opponent's near leg to prevent step-over escapes
Use hip elevation and movement to keep opponent off-balance and reactive
Create angles with body positioning to set up different sweep variations
Transition quickly when opponent's weight shifts to capitalize on openings

training_drills.name: Deep Half Entry Repetitions
training_drills.description: Partner starts in top half guard with forward pressure. Practice sliding underneath and establishing deep underhook, head position, and inverted body placement. Focus on smooth entry mechanics and maintaining tight underhook throughout.

training_drills.name: Sweep Chain Drill
training_drills.description: From established deep half guard bottom, partner defends one sweep attempt forcing transition to another sweep option. Practice linking Waiter Sweep → Old School Sweep → Rolling Back Take in response to opponent's defensive reactions.

training_drills.name: Positional Sparring from Deep Half
training_drills.description: Start in deep half guard bottom position. Bottom player works to sweep or take back while top player attempts to pass. Reset to deep half after each successful sweep or pass. Emphasize maintaining underhook control and creating angles.

execution_steps: 1. **Entry:** From Half Guard bottom, wait for the top player to drive weight forward — this is your entry trigger.
2. **Create space:** Frame on the opponent's hip with your free hand and shrimp your hips away to create space underneath them.
3. **Shoot under:** Drive your head and shoulders under the opponent's near hip, angling your body perpendicular to theirs.
4. **Establish deep underhook:** Wrap your top arm deeply around their far thigh, gripping behind their knee or upper hamstring — this is your primary control.
5. **Position your head:** Press your head against their inner thigh near the hip, creating a wedge that disrupts their base.
6. **Invert your body:** Roll your shoulders onto the mat with your hips elevated, body fully inverted underneath their center of gravity.
7. **Secure near-leg control:** Use your free hand or your legs to monitor and control the opponent's near leg, preventing step-over escapes.
8. **Elevate your hips:** Drive your hips upward into their center of mass to keep them constantly off-balance and reactive.
9. **Read their weight:** If they commit forward, execute the Waiter Sweep or Old School Sweep. If they try to step over, take the rolling back take.
10. **Execute sweep:** For Waiter Sweep — elevate with your hips and lift their far leg upward and forward while rolling them over your body.
11. **Follow through:** Maintain grip through the sweep and complete to Mount or Side Control depending on their defensive reaction.
12. **Transition to back if defended:** If they whizzer to defend, their arm is trapped — immediately enter the Electric Chair or roll for the back take.

faq.question: What is Deep Half Guard in BJJ?
faq.answer: Deep Half Guard is an advanced guard position where the bottom player slides their upper body underneath the opponent's hips, controlling the far leg with a deep underhook. Unlike standard Half Guard where you control from the side, Deep Half creates a leverage fulcrum using your shoulder and head against their inner thigh. The position is highly offensive despite appearing defensive — it generates powerful sweeps directly to Mount or Back Control.

faq.question: How do I enter Deep Half Guard?
faq.answer: Enter when the top player commits weight forward. Frame on their hip, shrimp to create space, then shoot your head and shoulders underneath their near hip. Establish the deep underhook of their far leg before they can react. Timing is critical — entering too early lets them defend, too late and they'll have already passed.

faq.question: What sweeps can I do from Deep Half Guard?
faq.answer: The primary sweeps are: (1) Waiter Sweep to Mount (beginner 30%, advanced 65%) — when opponent drives forward; (2) Old School Sweep to Side Control (beginner 35%, advanced 70%) — classic hip-lift sweep; (3) Rolling Back Take to Back Control (beginner 20%, advanced 60%) — when opponent steps over; (4) X-Guard Sweep to standing (beginner 25%, advanced 60%) — when opponent pulls far leg back.

faq.question: What is the difference between Deep Half Guard and regular Half Guard?
faq.answer: Regular Half Guard involves the bottom player controlling the opponent's near leg between their legs, maintaining a relatively vertical body position. Deep Half Guard requires inverting entirely underneath the opponent's hips with a deep underhook of their far leg. Deep Half trades positional exposure for powerful mechanical leverage — you are physically under your opponent's center of gravity, making sweeps more powerful but requiring more hip mobility and timing.

faq.question: Is Deep Half Guard good for beginners?
faq.answer: Deep Half Guard has a moderate learning curve. Sweep success rates start at 20-35% for beginners but rise significantly with practice. The entry timing is the hardest element to master. Beginners should first develop solid standard Half Guard, then learn the Deep Half entry. The position rewards patient practitioners — it's better suited to blue and purple belts than white belts, though the concepts can be introduced early.

faq.question: How do I escape Deep Half Guard when on top?
faq.answer: Escaping Deep Half top requires: (1) Immediately establish crossface to disrupt opponent's vision and sweep mechanics; (2) Widen your base with your free leg — think tripod stance; (3) Balance weight 50/50, avoiding forward lean (triggers Waiter Sweep) or backward lean (triggers Old School Sweep); (4) Methodically extract your trapped leg using gradual, controlled movement; (5) Complete the pass to Side Control before they reconstruct their grips.

faq.question: What is the Electric Chair from Deep Half Guard?
faq.answer: The Electric Chair is a submission used when the top player whizzers (overhooks your sweeping arm) to defend Deep Half sweeps. When they whizzer, their far arm is now trapped under yours. Establish Lockdown with your legs, then apply upward pressure with your legs while pushing their upper body away, creating a hyperextension on their hip and spine. It transitions into a split-the-legs position forcing a tap or sweep.

faq.question: Who developed Deep Half Guard in BJJ?
faq.answer: Deep Half Guard was pioneered and systematized in modern competition BJJ by Jeff Glover in the no-gi context, and further developed by Lucas Leite and Bernardo Faria in the gi. Bernardo Faria's entire competition game centered on Deep Half, winning multiple IBJJF World Championships using it as his primary guard. The 10th Planet system, created by Eddie Bravo, integrated Deep Half with Lockdown and Electric Chair into a comprehensive system.

expert_insights.danaher: Deep half guard represents a fundamental shift in guard philosophy - rather than controlling from the front, we control from below by removing the opponent's base entirely. The deep underhook of the far leg is non-negotiable; without it, the position ceases to function. The biomechanical advantage comes from creating a wedge with your shoulder and head against their inner thigh while maintaining an inverted position that allows you to lift their entire weight with your hips and core. Most beginners make the mistake of staying too flat - you must be inverted underneath their center of gravity to generate proper leverage. The position is a complete system with multiple sweep variations, but they all rely on the same fundamental principle: controlling the far leg while using hip elevation to disrupt their base. When entering, timing is critical - you need their weight committed forward before sliding underneath. The transition to back control via the rolling back take is particularly high percentage because it uses their defensive reactions against them.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: Deep half guard is one of the most reliable positions in competition, especially in no-gi where it's harder for opponents to establish grips to defend. I use it constantly when facing heavy pressure passers who want to smash - the harder they drive forward, the easier the sweeps become. The key is not to force the position too early; wait until they commit their weight, then slide underneath and establish the deep underhook. From there, I have four or five different sweeps I can hit depending on how they react. If they whizzer, I go to electric chair. If they post out wide, I hit the old school. If they try to step over, I take the back. The position is basically a trap - every defensive option they have opens up a different attack for me. In competition, I look for deep half especially after failed passing attempts when opponents are off-balance and looking to recover. One mistake I see all the time is people giving up the underhook too easily - you need to fight like hell to keep that far leg controlled because once it's gone, the position is finished.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: Deep half guard is straight-up one of the most powerful positions in jiu-jitsu, period. We've built an entire system around it in 10th Planet because it works at the highest levels and it's nearly impossible to shut down if you know what you're doing. The beautiful thing is that it's a position where you can be completely underneath someone and still be attacking - that's the mind game aspect that freaks people out. They think they're winning because they're on top, but really they're in your trap. The electric chair from deep half is money - when they whizzer to defend the sweep, boom, you've got the lockdown locked in and you're attacking their knee. Jeff Glover really pioneered this position in no-gi and showed everyone how deadly it could be. The key is staying loose and mobile underneath - you can't be stiff or you'll get smashed. You need to be able to move your hips, change angles, and create that elevation for the sweep. We drill this constantly because the entry timing is everything. Too early and they'll defend, too late and they'll have already passed. But when you time it right and get that deep underhook, you're in complete control even though you're underneath.

top.name: Deep Half Guard Top
top.description: Master Deep Half Guard Top with defensive counters, pressure maintenance, and systematic passing strategies. Success rates: Beginner 35%, Intermediate 55%, Advanced 70%.
top.overview:
Deep Half Guard Top is a challenging defensive position where you find yourself on top but with your opponent underneath in deep half guard, meaning they have wedged themselves deep under your hips with their arms around your far leg and their head/shoulders positioned under your near hip. While you are technically on top, this position presents significant sweep dangers and requires careful defensive strategy to maintain position and create passing opportunities.

The position is deceptive because the top player appears to be winning, but deep half guard is actually a highly effective sweeping position for the bottom player. Your opponent's deep positioning under your hips creates powerful leverage for sweeps, particularly the waiter sweep and old school sweep, which can easily result in mount or back control for them if you don't defend correctly.

Success from top position requires understanding the sweep mechanics your opponent is attempting, maintaining proper weight distribution to counter these sweeps, and systematically working to extract your trapped leg and establish dominant passing pressure. Patience is essential, as rushing to pass without proper defensive positioning often results in sweeps or back exposure.
state_invariants: Opponent is positioned deep underneath your hips with their body inverted or perpendicular to yours, their shoulders and head creating a wedge under your near-side hip while they control your far leg with their arms wrapped around the thigh or knee
Your trapped leg is controlled by opponent's arms with their shoulder pressure preventing easy extraction, while your free leg maintains base contact with the mat to prevent being swept

Weight distribution is balanced between both legs to prevent opponent from utilizing leverage to execute sweeps, with your torso maintaining upright or slightly forward posture to avoid being flattened

Opponent's head position is underneath or beside your hip creating the fulcrum for potential sweep mechanics, requiring constant monitoring and defensive adjustment to prevent activation of sweep leverage
prerequisites: Opponent has successfully entered deep half guard from half guard bottom, lockdown, or open guard recovery
Opponent has established deep positioning with their shoulders underneath your hips and secured control of your far leg
You are on top but with compromised base due to opponent's deep underhook and hip positioning
Opponent has created the leverage structure necessary for sweep attempts while you maintain some degree of upright posture
key_principles: Weight Distribution Management: Maintain balanced weight to prevent both waiter and old school sweeps
Trapped Leg Extraction Priority: Systematically work to free your trapped leg as it's the key to escaping
Crossface Control: Establish crossface or head control to limit opponent's ability to execute sweep mechanics
Posture Maintenance: Keep good posture and avoid being flattened or broken down
Base Widening: Use free leg to establish wide base that makes you difficult to off-balance
Grip Fighting: Prevent opponent from establishing sweep grips on belt or pants
Patience Under Pressure: Recognize this is dangerous position requiring methodical escape

common_errors.error: Explosive or forceful movements to free trapped leg
common_errors.consequence: Creates off-balancing forces that facilitate sweeps. Opponent uses momentum against you for sweeps, often resulting in being swept to mount or having back taken
common_errors.correction: Remain calm and methodical. Work gradual leg extraction while maintaining proper weight distribution and base. Small, controlled movements rather than explosive ones. Focus on crossface first, then leg extraction

common_errors.error: Incorrect weight distribution (too far forward or too far back)
common_errors.consequence: Placing too much weight forward enables waiter sweep; too much weight back enables old school sweep. Poor weight distribution is primary cause of sweeps from deep half top
common_errors.correction: Maintain balanced weight distribution - roughly 50/50 or slight preference forward with proper base. Constantly monitor and adjust based on opponent's sweep attempts. Widen base with free leg to create stability

common_errors.error: Allowing opponent to maintain head position deep under hip without pressure
common_errors.consequence: Opponent's head acts as fulcrum for sweep mechanics. Without disrupting this position, all their sweeps become high-percentage
common_errors.correction: Immediately establish crossface or head control to flatten opponent and disrupt their ability to look up. Use forearm or hand to apply pressure on their head, pushing it away from centerline

common_errors.error: Narrow base with free leg positioned close to body
common_errors.consequence: Makes you easy to off-balance and sweep. Limited base means any leverage opponent applies will move you
common_errors.correction: Widen base dramatically with free leg, posting it far to the side. Think tripod stance with free leg, trapped leg, and posting hand/arm creating wide stable base

common_errors.error: Staying in deep half top too long without systematically working to improve position
common_errors.consequence: Time favors the bottom player in deep half. The longer you stay, the more opportunities they have to perfect their grips and execute sweeps
common_errors.correction: Have systematic escape plan and execute it methodically. Work crossface, base establishment, leg extraction, and pass in sequence. If one path blocked, switch to alternate escape but maintain forward progress

training_drills.name: Deep Half Escape Flow Drill
training_drills.description: Partner enters deep half guard while you practice systematic escape sequence: establish crossface, widen base with free leg, shift weight forward slightly, extract trapped leg, and pass to side control. Start slow and focus on proper mechanics. Partner provides moderate resistance. Reset and repeat 10 times per side.

training_drills.name: Weight Distribution Sensitivity Drill
training_drills.description: Partner is in deep half guard and signals which sweep they're setting up (waiter or old school) by tapping your leg. You must adjust weight distribution to counter that specific sweep before they execute it. Develops sensitivity to sweep mechanics and proper defensive weight placement. 20 repetitions per side.

training_drills.name: Deep Half Defensive Sparring
training_drills.description: Positional sparring starting in deep half guard top. You work to pass while partner works to sweep. Reset every sweep or pass. Focus on maintaining calm defensive posture and systematic escape rather than explosive movements. 3-minute rounds with 1-minute rest.

execution_steps: 1. **Assess the threat:** Immediately identify that your opponent is in deep position — their head is near your far hip and they have underhook of your far leg.
2. **Widen your base:** Post your free leg wide to the side (tripod stance), creating maximum base stability before they can activate sweep mechanics.
3. **Establish crossface:** Drive your forearm or hand across their face/head, pushing their head away from your centerline — this disrupts their vision and lever position.
4. **Check your weight:** Balance 50/50 between both legs. Avoid forward lean (activates Waiter Sweep) and backward lean (activates Old School Sweep).
5. **Control their near leg:** Their near leg is trapped between yours — ensure it stays controlled to prevent them from creating angles with their legs.
6. **Fight the underhook:** Prevent their deep underhook grip from tightening. Use your near arm to clamp down on their grip or strip it.
7. **Apply shoulder pressure:** Drive your near-side shoulder down into their upper back or head to flatten them and reduce their inversion leverage.
8. **Begin leg extraction:** With crossface and base established, begin slowly extracting your trapped leg using circular hip movement, not explosive force.
9. **Switch to passing:** As you extract the leg, immediately step it over to set up your chosen pass — Crossface Pass or Knee Slice Pass.
10. **Recognize the Kimura:** If they overcommit their underhook arm to grip-fight, their arm is exposed for Kimura from Half Guard — attack opportunistically.
11. **Complete to Side Control:** Once the leg clears, drive your weight through and consolidate Side Control before they can recover guard.
12. **Prevent re-entry:** After passing, maintain hip pressure and crossface to stop them from attempting another deep half entry.

faq.question: How do I stop someone from entering Deep Half Guard?
faq.answer: Prevent deep half entry by: (1) Never committing your weight fully forward in Half Guard — keep balanced distribution; (2) Establish and maintain crossface early to prevent the opponent from inverting; (3) Post your far leg back when you feel them beginning to slide under; (4) Control their inside shoulder to block the inversion. Prevention is significantly easier than escaping — these habits should become automatic in all Half Guard top sequences.

faq.question: What is the best pass from Deep Half Guard top?
faq.answer: The Crossface Pass is the highest-percentage option from Deep Half Guard top (beginner 35%, advanced 70%). Establish a strong crossface with your near arm, widen your base, then systematically extract your trapped leg while maintaining shoulder pressure. The Knee Slice Pass is a strong alternative (advanced 65%) when the opponent's guard is less deep. Both require methodical execution rather than explosive force.

faq.question: Why is it dangerous to be on top in Deep Half Guard?
faq.answer: Deep Half Guard is deceptive — you appear to be winning from top position, but the bottom player has created a lever system using your own body weight against you. Their shoulder acts as a fulcrum under your hip, and any weight shift activates high-percentage sweeps: forward lean triggers the Waiter Sweep to Mount (60% success for experienced players), backward lean triggers the Old School Sweep to Side Control (55%). The position strongly favors the bottom player despite appearances.

faq.question: Should I use explosive movements to escape Deep Half Guard top?
faq.answer: Explosive movements are counterproductive when escaping Deep Half Guard top. Any sudden force creates momentum that skilled bottom players will redirect into sweep attempts — they are trained to use your explosiveness against you. Instead, use slow, controlled, methodical extraction: establish your crossface, widen your base, then gradually work your leg free. Patience and proper structure are more effective than strength.

expert_insights.danaher: Deep half guard top represents one of the most deceptive positions in grappling - you appear to be winning because you're on top, but the reality is quite different. The bottom player has created a sophisticated lever system using your body weight against you, with their shoulders acting as the fulcrum underneath your hips. Understanding the biomechanics of the primary sweeps from deep half is essential for defensive success. The waiter sweep activates when your weight shifts too far forward, allowing them to lift and rotate you over their shoulder. The old school sweep works when your weight is too far back, enabling them to roll you backward over your own base. Your defensive strategy must center on weight distribution that negates both sweep mechanisms simultaneously, which requires balanced positioning with neither too much forward nor backward lean. The systematic escape involves establishing a crossface to disrupt their vision and sweep mechanics, widening your base with the free leg to create stability, and methodically extracting the trapped leg while maintaining proper weight distribution. This is not a position for explosive movements - every sudden motion creates momentum that skilled practitioners will redirect into sweep attempts.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: I view deep half top as a temporary defensive position that I need to escape from as quickly as possible, but quickly doesn't mean frantically. When I end up there, my first priority is preventing the sweep - I widen my base, establish crossface or head control, and make sure my weight distribution doesn't give them the sweep they want. Then I systematically work to free my leg and pass. The worst thing you can do is rush the pass attempt, because that's when you get swept or give up your back. If the opponent is really good at deep half, I might even accept spending 30 seconds or a minute methodically escaping rather than risking a sweep by being impatient. The key is recognizing that time isn't necessarily against you if you're maintaining good defensive structure - it's only against you if you're in bad position getting attacked. Once I establish crossface and proper base, I'm controlling the pace and working my escape on my terms. In competition, I've seen so many people get swept from deep half because they panic and try to explode out. Stay calm, maintain your structure, and systematically improve your position step by step.
